title: How to compare the best brunch catering companies in Dubai
focus: Ask how each provider balances prepared food with dishes finished on site. A live egg station can be appealing, but it needs appropriate facilities and a plan for guest arrivals. Compare pastries, fruit, savoury choices and dietary alternatives as a complete meal. Confirm the drinks service and the equipment included. A clear proposal explains how the table will stay comfortable throughout the brunch, rather than simply presenting a long list of breakfast dishes.

sections.title: Use the same questions for every provider
paragraphs: A comparison becomes more useful when each proposal answers the same brief. Give providers a consistent guest count, venue, service time and menu direction. Ask them to identify preparation, delivery, equipment, staffing and clear-down separately enough for you to understand the complete scope.

Look for evidence relevant to your occasion. A portfolio may show a style you like, but ask how that format would work at your venue and for your group. If a particular credential or operational capability is essential, request the relevant information rather than assuming it from general marketing language.

There is no universal best option for every event. Compare the clarity of the proposal, the suitability of the menu and the practical plan alongside the price. A provider who understands the brief and explains responsibilities clearly gives you a stronger basis for deciding how your event will be catered.

sections.title: Give the menu a clear direction
paragraphs: Begin with a few dishes or flavours that your guests will enjoy, then build a balanced selection around them. A strong menu includes variety in texture, colour and richness without trying to cover every possible preference with a separate dish. The most useful question is how the food will work as a complete meal or reception.

Consider the time of day and the length of service. A short welcome reception needs a different amount and style of food from an evening where canapés replace dinner. Similarly, a working lunch should be easy to serve and enjoy within the available break.

Menu examples are a starting point for discussion. Ingredients, dietary variations and the practical requirements of your venue need to be reviewed before the final selection is confirmed. That gives the team room to recommend food that suits the occasion and can be served well.

sections.title: Build the service schedule around your guests
paragraphs: Work backwards from the time guests should begin eating. The team may need access earlier for unloading, setup and preparation, particularly when equipment or several service areas are involved. Share the programme before the menu is finalised so the catering plan can support it.

Identify moments when service should pause, such as a speech, presentation or ceremony. For an office event, confirm the length of each break and whether everyone will arrive at once. For a private celebration, allow for the welcome period and any cake or toast that needs its own place in the sequence.

Agree a contact for changes on the day. Small timing adjustments may be manageable, while a substantial extension can affect staffing and the booked hours. Clear communication helps the team respond sensibly and keeps the food connected to the occasion rather than running on a separate timetable.

sections.title: List the equipment before calling the plan complete
paragraphs: Food, kitchen equipment and table items are separate parts of a catering brief. Confirm what the venue supplies and what the catering team needs to bring. Depending on the format, that may include preparation equipment, holding equipment, serving utensils, crockery, glassware or linen.

A photograph of a styled event does not establish what is included in your own package. If you want the same type of table setup or service display, ask for those items to be identified in the proposal. This is particularly useful when the property has limited kitchen facilities or the event uses more than one dining area.

Also agree how equipment will arrive, be set up and be collected. Access restrictions and collection times can affect the plan. A clear equipment list helps the team prepare properly and gives you a practical way to check that the venue is ready before guests arrive.

sections.title: Give beverages their own service plan
paragraphs: Tell us whether you need only food or would also like drinks service included. Water, soft drinks, coffee, tea and mocktails each create different preparation and replenishment needs. A self-service drinks station may suit one event, while another benefits from a dedicated hospitality professional.

For a larger gathering, consider where guests will collect drinks and how used glasses or cups will be cleared. Ice, refrigeration, glassware and waste handling should be included in the discussion rather than assumed to come with the menu. The service needs to remain practical throughout the event, not only when the first drinks are poured.

Any request involving alcohol depends on the venue and the permitted arrangements and must be confirmed separately. The written scope should make clear what is supplied, what the client or venue provides and which staffing is included. This keeps the beverage plan aligned with the rest of the occasion.

sections.title: Compare the complete proposal
paragraphs: Read the price together with the menu and service scope. Two proposals can have different totals because one includes equipment, staffing or a longer service period that the other does not. Compare them against the same guest count and requirements before deciding which is the better fit.

Check the minimum order, included hours, delivery or transport arrangements and how applicable VAT is shown. If the menu uses a starting price, ask which choices could change it. Premium ingredients, additional stations, extended service and extra hospitality support may need separate pricing.

The written proposal should also explain the payment schedule and the terms for changes or cancellation. Use the terms attached to your booking, as a private occasion and a corporate contract may have different arrangements. A clear comparison gives you confidence in the decision and helps avoid assumptions about what a headline price includes.

sections.title: A clear brief gives the menu a better starting point
paragraphs: Start with the date, venue and number of guests, then describe how you want the occasion to feel. A working lunch, an evening reception and a family celebration need different menus and service rhythms. Tell us when people will eat, whether they will be seated or standing and which parts of the event you would like myCHEF to handle.

Include essential dietary requirements and the facilities available at the venue. A brief does not need to be long, but it should distinguish what is essential from what would simply be nice to have. If you have a spending range, share it alongside the scope so the proposal can prioritise the right elements.

We can then discuss a suitable format, food selection and staffing plan. Your written proposal brings those decisions together, giving you a clear reference for what is included before you confirm the booking.
